title: Salok Sehskriti
hookLine: verses in a Sanskrit-flavored style, on the passing world (ang 1353)

cards: Some words wear a robe. Say thou instead of you, or hath instead of has, and the room changes: the sentence sounds older, like it came from a temple instead of a kitchen.

Near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib, from Ang thirteen hundred fifty-three, sits a set of verses that does exactly that. They're called Salok Sehskriti, and their words wear the robe of an old learned language.
Today, just listen to how it sounds.

teach.b: Sehskriti, sometimes spelled Sahaskriti, names the style. Call it Sanskrit-flavored; that's the plain way to say it. These are not verses in classical Sanskrit, but speech dressed in its endings and its weight.
Lines close on sounds like ang and ah, so the ear hears something stately and old.
Guru Nanak's saloks open the set, and Guru Arjan's verses follow. Here's the surprise. Sanskrit was the language of learned pandits and temple scholarship.
On the pages around these verses, the Gurus sing in the speech of ordinary people. Here they pick up the learned register instead. Why?
The text doesn't explain itself. Some readers suggest it speaks to the learned in their own manner.
Others hear it simply as range: the Guru can sing in the village voice and the scholar's voice, and say the same truth in both. And what the verses say in that robe isn't new.
Paraphrased, they keep turning to how quickly this world passes, and how only remembering the Lord stays.
Grand dress, and the message Sikhs hear all through the Granth.
A learned language doesn't make the Name truer, and a plain one doesn't make it smaller. The Guru wears whichever robe reaches the listener.

how: The Salok Sehskriti of Guru Nanak and Guru Arjan are part of the closing sections of the Guru Granth Sahib; they are read in full during an akhand path or sahaj path, and some Sikhs study them with a giani's help because of their unusual vocabulary.

games.q: you're a Guru with a truth to sing, and the learned of your day speak a grand, old language. what do the Salok Sehskriti do?
o: refuse that language and use only plain speech.
pick up the learned style and say the same truth in it.
invent a new teaching to suit the grand style.
games.why: the Gurus wear the learned robe here, and the message underneath is the same one sung in the people's speech.

practice: If you can find the Salok Sehskriti, from Ang thirteen hundred fifty-three, read two of them aloud, slowly, in Gurmukhi or transliteration, and listen to the endings and the weight of the sound rather than chasing every word.
If you can't find them, listen to the plainest sound near you, a fan, a bird, traffic, and notice that it, too, is a voice. Then let the sound fade into the breath.
